389.t: Freelancing after Whiteman and working for Nat Shilkret
389.s: He wrote for Willard Robinson and Don Voorhees but mostly for Nat Shilkret's radio work for about three years.
389.ch: Freelance and studio work in New York
389.q: Well, I got out of the Whiteman band and I called up Nat or Nat called me up, heard about it and he wanted to know if I'd do some work in the radio and I had been in touch -- I ran into Willard Robinson Rose and he asked me if I would do some things for him and his Deep River orchestra. Bill had…

389.t: Office job in the 1960s and television work for Bernie Green
389.s: He spent over a year as a cement company dispatcher while still doing some TV orchestrations for Bernie Green.
389.q: Well, I think I did the Ethel Merman and what's her name, the girl from Texas, Mary Martin, and the Ethel Merman show. That was special.

389.s: He praises Bernie Green's method of handing him sketches for TV specials, including the Martin and Merman show.
389.q: Oh, Bernie particularly. He was very sharp on his -- he would get together with the talent and with the director of the show, and he was a very capable musician, orchestrator as well as composer, at least TV composer.

389.t: Mark Warnow and the Lucky Strike formula
389.s: His arrangement for Lucky Strike worked without brass in the first chorus, and the director rejected the experiment.
389.q: That's right. Now, back further there was -- the guy that used to have the Lucky Strike. He used to like my work too. Not his brother --

389.t: The Kate Smith show: every section must be heard
389.s: The show demanded sixteen bars featuring every brass and sax player, and he admits he was an unsuccessful radio orchestrator.
389.q: The same thing would happen on the Kate Smith Show, which I did for three years. I remember one time changing what they wanted -- you know, what they wanted was Kate Smith sings the first chorus, and then for 16 bars you've got to bring the orchestra in, and they had four trumpets, four trombones.…

389.t: Working for Nat Shilkret on radio
389.s: Shilkret was more of a musician, never cut him down, and the Saturday evening show had good sidemen but lasted one season.
389.q: But this was the -- now, with Shilkret Shoret it was a little different. Shoret was more of a musician, and he was a little bit more of that style of the '20s. That's when he came up also.

389.t: Bix on a big NBC radio band and the director who interfered
389.s: When Bix, back from Davenport, joined a Shilkret radio show, a director hovered over his solo and he was soon off the show.
389.ch: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
389.q: Well, he could have been. I know he did a lot of the work that Nat had, and Nat had these shows, and there was one there that they passed on that Bix got onto. That was a guy who -- who later went out to the Coast. He's in all the books, but I -- it was the Camel Pleasure -- it was

389.t: Radio background music and the Kate Smith dramas
389.s: Radio increasingly wanted dramatic background music, which he could not do for Kate Smith's dramas.
389.q: So, when I got out, and with doing radio work, I found out that the music, the type of music they were playing were backgrounds. Everything was a background. If you wanted to work, there were any number of guys that could sit down and write a background to a story. Bernie Green was

389.t: A Detroit beer program and Phil Wall's quick arrangements
389.s: A sponsor told him not to educate listeners with divided strings, and he would not copy Phil Wall's fast formula arrangements.
389.q: Now, this is a case where I didn't have exact instructions, but I think what they figured is I should have known better, because I'd worked on the Lucky Strike before. I had another experience with a guy who used -- who used to do a beer program out in Detroit. He used to go out there and do

389.t: Arranger versus orchestrator: radio cuts and commercial breaks
389.s: By the 1930s radio dictated brief orchestrations that were cut for announcements, unlike his freer 1920s arranging.
389.q: Yes. During the '20s I was -- I was an arranger to set up something, maybe some sort of a style, to contribute any way I could. They were willing to accept that, and I did my work as I thought best. In other words, they gave me a tune to arrange. When the business -- when it came to 19 -- in the…

389.t: Radio arranging pace: Bargy and Hayden versus Grofe and Challis
389.s: Bargy and Hayden turned out many fast arrangements for extra pay while Challis and Grofe plodded along at two a week.
389.q: Now, he had to look forward to the radio business. The dance business had gone by and in this radio thing, you know, we weren't -- Ferde and I both, we were not used to that either. We were not you know, "Get this out by 8 o'clock." We were not used to that sort of thing. Barby and Lenny, they were…

108.t: The variety of ABC work and the staff orchestras
108.s: Opera auditions, Voice of Firestone, dance-party imitations of bands and brass quintet; networks employed ninety-five musicians.
108.q: He set a certain tone there. Everybody deported himself in a very dignified manner. The people who ran the American Broadcasting Company were highly respectful of him, and consequently they treated the musicians with great respect, and he, in turn, demanded that the musicians respect the job and so…

108.t: A typical week on staff at ABC
108.s: Hired about 1957, he works up to three shows a week from a posted schedule.
108.q: It depended on – no, you might do as many as three in the week. You might do a radio show or two radio shows, and you might have a television show to do. Or sometimes you just did one thing. You might just be assigned to one thing. You get your schedule. It would be posted. You’d go in and look at…

108.t: Scripted radio shows and subbing for Bobby Hackett
108.s: Script shows required short cues; he substitutes for Hackett.
108.q: This wasn’t a script show, of course. Ernie was doing his things, his comedy things. He’d take routines. He’d see something in the paper that had happened, and he’d make a whole story out of it. He did that. But then there were some shows, like soap­ opera-type things, where you had a script and…

108.t: Seventeen years at ABC and outside staff work
108.s: He stays on staff seventeen years and also does NBC and CBS shows.
108.q: 17 years, actually on staff, and I worked there for almost two years prior to that as an outside player. During that time, when I as on staff, when we had nothing – if we had nothing to do, Mr. Vagnoni was very nice about that. He’d say – sometimes, for instance, you might be scheduled for…

108.t: Subbing on The Tonight Show and other TV shows
108.s: He subbed under Allen, Parr, and Carson, and played other shows.
108.q: Oh, I was cutting my own throat. I did – I don’t know if I mentioned to you. I did – when The Tonight Show – I did that show as a substitute when – what’s-his-name was there. Who was there? Before Jack Parr – Steve Allen.

108.s: Kovacs's pranks, firecracker and cheesecake throwing.
108.q: That was great. Ernie was as entertaining to us as he was to the audience on the radio, and he loved musicians. He would come in – one morning, I remember in particular. It was the Fourth of July. The show was on the air from six in the morning until nine. So we would come in for rehearsal at five…

108.t: Staff orchestras at ABC and the networks
108.s: Wilder describes the network staff orchestras, their conductors, live broadcasts, the end of staffs by the mid-1970s, and discarded tapes.
108.q: I would think, well I guess it went from about the late 30’s through the 70’s. Because I think it was ‘75 when we stopped doing the Dick Cavett show, and at that point they had begun to get rid of the staff orchestras at all the networks.

108.t: The Dick Cavett Show and staff pay
108.s: He plays Cavett and Merv Griffin; staff pay was salaried and strings were kept on sustaining salary.
108.q: I did The Dick Cavett Show from the time it started until it went off the air. And I used to do – at ABC, on radio, we also did The Merv Griffin Show, when he had his show on radio. We did that.

108.t: Early mornings and playing the wrong tune
108.s: Five-day schedule at dawn and Wilder confidently plays the wrong song as a solo.
108.q: No, we didn’t – when we were doing that, that was during the week. That was – I think we did that five days. It didn’t run that long. It was on for a while, but it didn’t actually run that long. Then he went to NBC, I think, and started. But it was fun. Then you just got into that routine of being…

371.t: Radio in his childhood and jazz on the air
371.s: Canadian stations CKOK and CKOW and jazz's difficulty finding radio sponsors.
371.ch: Pontiac childhood, family and piano training
371.q: Well, there was a station called CKOK from Canada, and CKOW. They used to put a lot of Fats Waller records on later on, not at that time, but later on. But, that was the only station in the area, aspect of the second or maybe for five stations in Detroit like WJR, WWJ, WWJX Shortwave; they didn't…

371.t: Getting the CBS staff job through Andy Williams
371.s: Network staffs hired musicians; Jones got CBS in 1958-59 via summer shows with Andy Williams; conductors Ray Bloch and Erwin Cossel.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: The fact that ABC, CBS, and NBC were not recording studios but they hired musicians. They'll had staffs. When I first came to New York NBC had about 100 people on staff, NBC had 80 or 85. CBS had about 55 or 60 people on staff. So, the

371.t: A typical CBS week: rehearsals, tapings and the shows he covered
371.s: The routine of rehearsal, run-through and dress rehearsal for the Garry Moore show, later the Gleason and Sullivan shows.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: There I was a little time to freelance in between working days. A typical day at CBS started with a rehearsal day. You go into a studio in 57th St. at the production center and rehearse the music that you would be playing on the air, two days later., This is for the Gary Moore show. The rehearsal…

371.t: The 'modern jazz' radio show and CBS studios
371.s: A staff-based straight-ahead jazz radio show with Hal McKusick and Jimmy Nottingham, recorded in CBS radio studios, often without charts.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: Well, it wasn't called “Modern Jazz Show" that was the name they used. It wasn't a Dixieland, it was just on the show. We didn't play any Dixieland. They just called it "Modern Jazz," not to be confused with the Modern Jazz Quartet. But, it was straight-line jazz. It was mainline jazz kind of…

371.s: Gleason was a jazz fan involved in every aspect of the production, and invited Jones to play golf.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: I did you do that show. I think she appeared on the Gary Moore show once or twice. But, I think she had her show of her own. I think she was on ABC, or NBC. I'm not sure.

371.s: Jones played a few times on the Today Show with a small group, before CBS.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: That was NBC. I did that as a gas on a small group with Mandel Lowell sometimes. There was also George Duvivier and Dave Garroway. One Dave Garroway used do the show, I did it a couple times. I did it one time after Dave left. But, that was with NBC. That was actually before I started work at CBS.…

371.t: His workload: auditions and the Arthur Godfrey show
371.s: Jones spent a five-day week on shows, TV casting auditions and Godfrey rehearsals.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: I had three days in the studio including rehearsals – – I used to also do auditions. I forgot to tell you that. I used to work out of TV casting. Being a pianist, I used to have to go and play auditions if I worked out of casting, at the casting office. Singers would come down there to audition for…

371.s: Jones played a Dixieland radio show with staff players and guests like Pee Wee Russell and Jack Teagarden, learning the style by ear.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: No, it’s not Peanuts Huckle, I know that name. He is a clarinetist. But it was Pee Wee Russell and some of the Dixieland players. Some of the guys were on staff, but they brought some guys into play that show. Jack Teegarden came through and played once– actually, a couple of times.

371.t: Board of Governors of the Academy of Television Arts
371.s: Jones joined in 1964 on a recommendation, found the meetings more social than productive, and left in 1971.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: I was recommended by one of the owners of a recording studio. He knew that I worked at CBS I guess if he felt that it was a good way for Afro Americans to break into this kind of thing. I was the only one representing musicians on staff there. Well the only one who was a member of that group. What…

384.t: Howard Lanin, Don Voorhees and joining NBC
384.s: Hutto lists his late-1920s recording and NBC work; Nat Shilkret is named as the director he worked for most, and he made many records with Victor Young.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: Nat Schilkret was one of them. And although he didn't know jazz at all. He'd have to take our word for what's good jazz. So Nat Schilkret, I think was the - I worked for him more than anyone else. He liked me, on account of my easy going way, my pace. He liked my pace. So that was it.

384.s: Hutto asks about the November 1937 audition record; Morehouse recalls only that it had the cream of NBC's musicians and was for NBC programs.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: No, this is strictly for the NBC programs. And they said Chauncey Morehouse and his N'goma band, you know. And that meant my turn was coming up. And then I would play two or three tunes and that would be it.

384.t: NBC exclusivity, the Fred Allen show and Peter Van Steeden
384.s: He was told by radio management he belonged to them; he played the Fred Allen show with Peter Van Steeden's band for years.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: Because when I got into radio, I talked to a big shot in the radio and he says 'now look, you can't be wandering around here doing work for everybody. You belong as of this moment to us. And we will tell you what to do. We'll keep you working. But you'll play what we tell you to play.'

384.t: Radio in the forties: Telephone Hour and Voice of Firestone
384.s: He cannot pin down his NBC staff status in the war years but played the Telephone Hour for Don Voorhees and several Voice of Firestone programs.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: You know I'd have to look that up. I really couldn't tell you. But I was with NBC for a hell of a long time. And I don't really remember now because life was going by and I just couldn't remember everything I was connected with.

384.t: Don Voorhees, the Rain or Shine show and radio work in 1928
384.s: After the New Yorkers he joined Don Voorhees, playing the Broadway show Rain or Shine and NBC radio, and also worked with Sam Lanin.
384.ch: Studio recordings of the late twenties and thirties
384.q: Yeah, radio it was. It was down here, somewhere between here and here.

384.t: The Swing Six and the 1937 NBC audition band
384.s: Kline lists the Swing Six personnel and Hutto discusses the November 1937 NBC audition record and his forgotten theme song for a sustaining orchestra.
384.ch: Bands, leaders and radio of the thirties and forties
384.q: I played for the jazz dance.

384.t: Forties and fifties radio: Merry Macs, Peter Van Steeden and Fred Allen
384.s: Having become an outside man who took any work, he played vibes with the Merry Macs and for seven years on the Fred Allen show with Peter Van Steeden.
384.ch: Bands, leaders and radio of the thirties and forties
384.q: An outside man is a man who takes anything that comes his way.

384.t: Hobby Lobby, Major Bowes and the Goldkette gong
384.s: Hutto recalls Morehouse's 1938 appearance on Hobby Lobby with the N'goma drums and on Major Bowes's Capitol Theater hour; a gong from Charlie Horvath sounds.

384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: Well Larry Clinton came into the NBC because his records were selling. And NBC wanted a guy whose records Could sell. So that's why they got him.

418.t: Fats Waller's radio show and the Ink Spots in Cincinnati
418.s: Fats Waller had the Rhythm Club show on WLW in Cincinnati, replaced by the Ink Spots, whose member Hoppy got his name there.
418.q: Which was taken from the Rhythm Club up here in Harlem. And I mean it was named after that you know. And he had a kind of act on there. That's when the first time the INK Spots got to be known.

418.t: Fats Waller's radio show and the Ink Spots in Cincinnati
418.s: Fats Waller had the Rhythm Club show on WLW, replaced by the Ink Spots, whose member Hoppy got his name there.
418.q: Yeah, he was staying in Cincinnati at the time. He had a show at WLW called "The Rhythm Club," which was taken from the Rhythm Club up here in Harlem -- I mean, it was named after that, you understand. And he had kind of an act on the air.

418.t: Fats Waller's radio show and the Ink Spots in Cincinnati
418.s: Fats Waller had the Rhythm Club show on WLW, replaced by the Ink Spots, whose member Hoppy got his name there.
418.ch: Early bands, Calloway to Basie and Kansas City (third typescript)
418.q: Which was taken from the Rhythm Club up here in Harlem. And I mean it was named after that you know. And he had a kind of act on there. That's when the first time the INK Spots got to be known.

418.t: Working with Fats Waller and Clarence Page in Cincinnati
418.s: Fats Waller did a radio show and used Clarence Page's band for outside work, with Una Mae Carlisle also in the band; Dickenson found Fats fun to work with.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: No, he did a radio... He was doing a radio show, and he had three or four characters on there. But after the show, he had a lot of work outside, and he used a band -- and I was in there playing.

418.t: Speed Webb broadcast locally but never recorded
418.s: Speed Webb's band broadcast locally but never made records or came to New York, which is why it was not a success.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: around the vicinity. But we just didn't get a chance. We didn't get a chance to make records or anything. That's why that band wasn't a success. We didn't make records. And we didn't come to New York.

418.t: Remote band broadcasts from the Cotton Club and Roseland
418.s: He wishes bands were again broadcast live from clubs and hotels as in the old days.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: I think those were great days. I think they should bring that back, and broadcast the bands from places that...certain nightclubs and things. People will be listening to that. I remember when I used to listen for the Cotton Club or for Roseland Ballroom or different things

418.s: They check the time and talk about Lawrence Welk, Cher, Star Trek and the television schedule.
418.q: I don't look at those things. SUN I ain't looking at that. (Inaudible). I'd just as soon look at Lawrence Welk as look at that.

418.t: Television chatter and the Tony Awards

He sat at the bar, and said, “I think, if I’m not mistaken, I think I see a bad trumpet player back there – flugelhorn player.” I said, “Unless my eyes are playing a trick on me, I think that’s old Bebop…

101.t: The Urban League and becoming NBC's first Black staff musician
101.s: The Urban League pressures NBC; Terry leaves Free and Easy in Paris to take the staff job.
101.q: In a sense, yeah, because there were not a whole hell of a lot of black musicians who were doing the jingle scene. During the time that I went at NBC – that’s when I first became – Gwen’s probably got some old checks around here that – I had kept a whole stack of them, all my NBC salary, which was…

101.t: Bringing Snooky Young onto the NBC staff
101.s: Terry recommends Snooky Young and both have to be immaculate to test their place.
101.q: That’s right, yeah. You have to understand now. Each network has 175 musicians. So this went on beautifully for a while, and the Urban League pressured them a little more. Said, “I think you can do a little better than that.” So now, Aaron

101.t: Terry's ultimatum to Aaron Levine over Snooky
101.s: Terry threatens a Johnson Publications story and the firing is dropped.
101.q: Yeah, right. I’m in the office of Aaron Levine at NBC, who was contractor of musicians at NBC, and he’s telling me all these details about why Snooky Young was not wanted there any longer. Skitch didn’t like him. He was doing this and that. I know that Skitch loved him, and everybody there loved…

101.t: Skin-color casting: Volkswagen ad and the Snader film
101.s: Milt Hinton replaces Barksdale for the ad; Marshal Royal replaces DeFranco on the Basie film; laughing to keep from crying.
101.q: Yeah, Cleve. Yeah, man, that was way back. I couldn’t remember. When you list the people, I can remember them now. Snooky, me, Cleve, Craw, Ernie. There were 10 of us. I can’t believe that all 10 got out of there playing instruments. But we did the music, and then we got ready to film, and the cats…

101.t: Passed over to lead The Tonight Show band
101.s: A producer's wife reveals executives thought a Black leader would hurt the Southern market.
101.q: I was up for the job. The reason I know I was up for the job: the lady who married Johnny’s producer, Rudy Tellez. Her name was Jeannie, I think. She was a friendly, beautiful little girl, and she befriended the guys, and particularly Snooky and me, because she knew what a hardship it was for us to…

101.t: Comparing NBC musicians and the threat to fire Snooky
101.s: Black players were fully qualified; Terry begins his ultimatum to the contractor.
101.q: There was no comparison. There were people of my color who could do anything that any one of them there had done, and in most instances, better. It was all a big . . .

101.t: Doc Severinsen gets The Tonight Show job
101.s: Terry and Severinsen talk about the racial reason; they laughed about it.
101.q: There was no issue between us, because we were both well aware of the situation, the racial situation. That’s the way it was, and there wasn’t a whole heck of a lot that you could do about it.

412.t: Refusing to play Woody Herman and Lu Watters records
412.s: Hodes talks about the Woody Herman oranges and refusing to play Lu Watters records. He says the producers insisted he follow scripts and he lost them while keeping the show.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: But this is what started our -- underneath, you know, because Leonard was not the kind of fellow to forgive and forget. The same thing with Woody Herman, but I never got any bad vibes from Woody. And in fact, they sent me a crate of oranges, which I ate, gladly. But never played Woody on the…

412.t: The Jazz Alley series and its guests
412.s: The series Jazz Alley used Chicago men to back guests such as Barney Bigard and Pee Wee Russell. It was shown on 205 stations.
412.q: So then we started doing Chicago things, and using Chicago men to back guests. So I used different people that would play. And brought in Barney Bigard and Doc Evans before he died. Pee Wee Russell was on before he died, Jimmy McPartland Eddie Condon before he died, Bud Freeman, besides J. C.…

412.t: The worst Jazz Alley show with Eddie Condon
412.s: Hodes says the worst show was with Condon, Tony Parenti and others. A two-hour intermission and tired players made it bad.
412.q: Now, Smokey played his butt off, played beautifully. And Tony Parenti, in spite of the fact that he was tired, played. But J.C. hadn't been playing, leaning up against the piano, he was tired. And that trip, they came from work without sleep. And then the engineer or somebody at the station, made a…

412.t: Losing the radio show to La Guardia
412.s: Mayor La Guardia heard the show twice and the program was ended. Hodes would not answer thirty letters a day.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: I lost it because La had heard me again. The second time he heard it, there was nothing for me to do. He always went on the air before me. I followed all the symphony music, all the fire alarms that he chased and all that. He was a great one for chasing fires in New York. And all the things that he…

412.s: After the Daily News piece, Hodes asks about television. A man offers a chance at WTTW.
412.q: 'Tell It Like It Is.' And so I met Mr. Keegan or Hogan or -- and I asked him if he could open a door for me on television. See, I tried radio and Studs tried for me, but for me to do a program on radio, no, there's no place for me, unless you go out and get a sponsor.

412.t: The first WTTW shows and a payment dispute
412.s: Hodes took his jazz talk to WTTW, which had no money. A year later they paid him scale.
412.q: But I knew that I could do it with playing. But I still hadn't had it all together. Like, these schools got it all together for me. I even played for high school kids. In many halls, you're sitting with -- the back of your head is facing them, 200 kids all around you. And you can feel a tomato…

412.t: Plain Old Blues wins a Chicago Emmy
412.s: Hodes did a WTTW show called Plain Old Blues about the beat in the music. It won a Chicago Emmy.
412.q: I went up there and I did a show and I called it Plain Old Blues. That time, I had already recorded Plain Old Blues. Again, I sat down and talked about that it all started with a beat and I made a beat and I says, now the beat appeared "A Closer Walk with.." in spirituals and I played -- it…

412.t: The WNYC radio show and the complaint that he was commercial
412.s: Hodes describes his WNYC radio program, where a station manager complained he was commercial. He kept the show anyway, and says listeners still remember it.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: Get that bum off the air, he's commercial. Now, I'm not getting a penny salary. I'm either buying my own records or they're being furnished to me. I'm paying my own carfare, I'm paying my own lunch. All they're doing is giving me an announcer and a turntable guy, that's there anyway. And this man…

88.t: CBS radio show with Rafael Mendez and a tuba Flight of the Bumblebee

88.t: Duke and Blanton on radio, and when Lee went on staff
88.s: Lee recalls Duke and Blanton on Bing Crosby's show and says he joined Columbia's staff in 1945 or 1946.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Louis used to do guest shots with Bing Crosby, and Duke used to do a lot of guest shots on radio, as a duo though. Duke and Jimmy Blanton. They used to do a lot of things on radio -- on big radio shows. You'd very often hear Blanton and Duke playing together.

88.t: Hired for the Camel Caravan then replaced the next week
88.s: After rehearsing and playing a CBS Camel Caravan show to congratulations, Lee returned the next Friday to find another drummer's set up.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: So I organized another little band that I had around town like 5 pieces, but in the midst of that, I got a call one day, one morning, early to come out to do the Camel Caravan -- it was the Camel Caravan Show -- right out here at CBS on Sunset Boulevard.

88.t: Freddie Fisher testifies for Lee; the cost and pioneering
88.s: Conductor Freddie Fisher appeared unasked to confirm hiring Lee; Lee was paid for 13 shows but felt the principle was unresolved.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Freddie Fisher surprised everyone. Freddie Fisher came to the Union. He was not supposed to be there, because they didn't tell him to come. But he heard about it, and he walked in, and he told -- he told them. He said, "He is the drummer that I hired. I told him that he had the job." He said,…

88.t: Turning down Bob Crosby's radio show on Dave Klein's advice
88.s: Offered three times the money on Bob Crosby's CBS show, Lee stayed on staff because Dave Klein said leaving would hurt the next black musician.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Oh yes, I went back to Columbia, and then I had an offer right across the street again, at CBS, Bob Crosby had a 15 minute -- was it the Chesterfield Show, wasn't it? Do you remember that? Bob Crosby had a 15 minute ... it was on 5 days a week.

88.t: Black musicians absent from radio except guest stars
88.s: Lee says he was the only black radio musician, apart from guests like Louis Armstrong with Bing Crosby.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: We had Louis -- he used to do a lot of things with Bing and that type of thing, when they had -- what's the big show that Bing and them had with ...

88.t: The DownBeat headline and the transfer rule violated for Nick Fatool
88.s: DownBeat headlined Color loses Lee Young's job; Lee believes it happened because of separate locals, since Nick Fatool took his job within days of arriving.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Freddie Fisher was his name. It came out in the DownBeat, May 1, 1943 in big red letters across the top of it, in bold type, it says "Color loses Lee Young's job" -- then it goes on to tell you, you know, what transpired, but I think one of the reasons a thing like that could happen at the time was…

388.t: Raymond Scott and his brother Mark Warnow on the Hit Parade
388.s: Leeman is offered a job on the Hit Parade after Raymond Scott took over his late brother Mark's conducting post, and Hinton praises their role in popular music.
388.q: Most grateful. So I worked with him, and about that year -- '51, I was approached, Raymond Scott, his brother had died and he acquired his brother's job on the Hit Parade.

388.t: Raymond Scott's quintet, Mitch Miller and Alec Wilder
388.s: Hinton and Leeman recall Raymond Scott's famous quintet and big band with Mitch Miller and Lou Shoobe, and the quintet playing the Jack Benny Show theme.
388.q: That was Mark -- that was Mark's band, his brother, before me. Because I ended up -- I finished a Hit Parade, I was just getting to that.

388.t: Working the Hit Parade in radio and early television
388.s: Leeman did the Hit Parade on Saturday for $180, but Nick's would not let him off, so he quit and became a freelance New York studio musician for six and a half years.
388.q: for a week's trial, a couple week's trial, and I wanted to do the show. I was making, which was very good money -- Nick's paid jazz musicians better than any other places around, which was $170 or $175 a week at that time.

388.t: Hackett friendship: Condon's Tuesday sessions and Jackie Gleason parties
388.s: Leeman sorts out dates, saying Hackett did not hire him until 1949-50, and recalls Condon's jam sessions, Gleason's private parties and Whiteman radio dates.
388.q: and I was out with the big bands, and when I returned to New York, Bobby didn't take me into Nicks in the Village, which had then moved over to 10th Street and 7th Avenue, he didn't take me in there until '49 and the first of '50. Not '39-'40.

388.t: Freelance work in early television and radio
388.s: On the strength of the Hit Parade, Leeman is hired as a freelance on the Perry Como, Jack Benny, Steve Allen and Telephone Hour shows, and works on 'You Are There' with Louis Armstrong.
388.q: However -- at this time, I was in to the Hit Parade, which I did on weekends, and my reputation was growing there. I was fortunate to be able to read and cut a few parts, and I was hired by contractors, I had a reputation of working on the Hit Parade, which was a great show in those days -- I was…

388.t: Doubling on Jackie Gleason's summer show and Elvis Presley's debut
388.s: Between Paramount shows the band cabs to Gleason's CBS show, where Leeman sees Elvis Presley's first major television appearance.
388.ch: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
388.q: In the meantime, Jackie Gleason had a big contract with CBS for the Gleason Show, and The Honeymooners. CBS gave him a summer replacement show -- I'm trying to recall the name of the show -- oh, the American Bandstand, I believe it was. And Gleason with his love for music and

388.t: Joining Raymond Scott's integrated CBS radio band
388.s: After leaving Woody, Leeman wins the drum job in Raymond Scott's CBS band with Ben Webster, Charlie Shavers and Milt Yaner, while Hinton and Leeman discuss who integrated CBS.
388.ch: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
388.q: No, it was the turning point. In the first place, when I left Woody, I was looking for a job, and I was walking down the street and I saw Cozy Cole, and he said Raymond Scott needs a drummer. And this was only a couple of days after I was without a job. So I went up and tried out for the job -- he…

150.t: From the Sentinel to radio: Richard Rising, WJBW and the Gladstone Hotel remote
150.s: He befriends WJBW announcer Richard Rising, is told the owners cannot put him on air in the studio, and becomes a part-time jazz disc jockey broadcasting remotes and selling his own time.
150.q: Well, from the Sentinel, what I did, like I told you, radio was coming in, in the focus at the time. And I ran into a young man by the name of Richard Rising, who was a white guy who was working at WJBW, radio station here on the corner of Camp and Canal. Well, I used to listen to Richard quite…

150.t: First black station WMRY in the French Quarter and its disc jockeys
150.s: After WJBW he joins WMRY with Ernie the Whip, Malcolm Brown, Bob Parker and Israel Augustine; an agency first pays him a salary, then the station hires him full time.
150.q: Well, after that, now, here comes WMRY, which is now WYLD. That's wild. WMRY started in the French Quarter by the Court of Two Sisters. Ernie Branger, who was Ernie the whip, he was the major black disc jockey down there. Well, Ernie and I had kept a beautiful relationship all of our lives because…

150.t: Dr. Daddy-O (Vernon Winslow) and his rise on WBOK
150.s: Tex recounts how Vernon Winslow, coaching white DJ Duke Thiel, got on the air, was sponsored by Jax beer, rose to fame, moved to WMRY and later declined.
150.q: All righty. You know, Ted, I think it's about time that we start talking about a young man who had one of the greatest radio trademarks ever in history.

150.t: Israel Augustine and the Sundown Supper Club program
150.s: Augustine worked evenings; Tex set up the Sundown Supper Club, easy jazz-flavored ballads, and WMRY moved to Dryades Street.
150.q: That was a slow type combination jazz, pop type of program. Like, Body and Soul, This Love of Mine, Over the Rainbow. Ballad. Ballad kind of thing. But in other words, easy listening music with jazz overtones. That's what it was all about.

150.t: Women, brewery sponsors and the perks of being a DJ
150.s: The DJs enjoyed attention from women and hospitality from brewing companies, 1950-62.
150.q: Oh, boy. It was a lot of fun. It was a lot of fun. We enjoyed ourselves. Oh, wow. Because you know, you didn't want to go crazy or nothing like that, because they had women everywhere, and they just wanted to take you home to dinner. And some women did, and some women took us out to cocktails at…

150.t: Tex's jazz-leaning radio show and early black radio
150.s: Tex describes his theme song, playing Woody Herman, Ellington, Basie and Gillespie, his patter, and the start of black radio and payola.
150.q: Well, you know, really, if you think about it, uh, if you think about it, when I first went on the end, uh, my, uh, theme song was Blue Flame by Woody Herman. And a lot of people say, well, here's a black dance jockey playing black, white music, but hell, I was a lover of the music that Woody…

324.t: How he met Steve Allen and the Regis Philbin Show
324.s: Allen was a fan; Gibbs became bandleader and second banana on the Regis Philbin Show with a sextet.
324.q: In fact that band, that size band is what I used when I was conducting with Steve. The sextet. With the clarinet, guitar and vibes, and piano, bass and drums.

324.t: Teaching Steve Allen vibes and conducting for him
324.s: Gibbs conducted for Allen for fifteen or sixteen years in clubs and TV, and teaches him vibes.
324.q: Oh let me get back to that, because you asked me how I got with Steve. Then Steve asked me if I would conduct for him. And I had another show coming up. By that time I was ready to sit down and settle down. No first he asked me actually if I would go to Las Vegas with him. Because I taught Steve…

324.t: Phone calls, then getting the Regis Philbin show gig after Steve Allen
324.s: Gibbs, a friend of Steve Allen, was hired as musical director for Regis Philbin's show on a 26-week contract.
324.q: Well I’ll tell you how it all started. I used to be — Steve Allen was my friend. I was friends with Steve in the early 40s, late 40s. He became my friend then he became a big fan of mine, you know. And when he got his TV show he got me as a guest all the time, I was a guest a lot. And we were doing…

324.t: Sextet choice, writing intros and endings, telethons, Basie and Eartha Kitt
324.s: Gibbs insisted on a sextet (Colin Bailey, Monty Budwig, Mike Melvoin, Herb Ellis), explains his intro-and-ending arranging trick and telethon system, and tells of Basie, Getz and Eartha Kitt on the show.
324.q: they said, “Okay we want you, it’s your job, but Steve Allen had a nine piece orchestra, we’ll give you a nine piece orchestra.” I said, “I don’t want it.” They said, “Well what do you mean?” I said, “You mean they give me a big band because we’re opposite Johnny Carson? Or opposite Elliot Lawrence…

324.t: Listening to band members' ideas, Operation: Entertainment
324.s: Gibbs says he is no control freak and took John Audino's suggestion on a tune order for Operation: Entertainment.
324.q: No, not at all. I mean you know what’s so wild? I listen to anybody in the band. For example I wrote all these things where I did a show called “Operation: Entertainment.” I had all these things follow me, a singer, a comedian, you know I had all these things I wrote for the band. And while we…

324.t: Memorizing music and losing his stand on the first show
324.s: Gibbs plays vibes from memory but on his first TV show stagehands took his music stand and he nearly missed a note.
324.q: I’ll tell you my first show, I’ve got to tell you this. You know I’m coming from New York and I was still a jazz musician and I’m getting called to do a TV show, I didn’t know anything about playing jazz so in my contract it had to be written that I would perform three times a week on camera with…

86.t: Hollywood Palace: three years in a vaudeville-style TV show
86.s: Under Mitchell Ayres he played acts and rotating hosts on a variety show, unlike a talk-show band.
86.q: Well, it was a variety show, like we'd have -- the Russians would send over the movies of an act with a cossack, the horses and all that. So we would have to look at that and put music to it, you know.

86.t: Talk-show bands and the Palace's guest hosts
86.s: Dance and Edison discuss the role of Johnny Carson's band, then Edison lists stars who hosted the Palace.
86.q: And when they have singers come on the show, they back the singers, you know, like -- and the band is a part of the show now.

86.t: Pay and schedule of the Hollywood Palace and other TV shows
86.s: Edison explains TV pay compared with life on the road with Basie, his rehearsal hours and the other shows he worked.
86.q: Well, to tape the show and rehearse would be -- we would do that on Thursday. We'd go on about 2:00 in the afternoon. We'd get out around eight, nine at night. That was rehearsal. Then the next day, we would have to be there -- well, it depended on how much music that we had to play. Then if we had…

86.t: The Camel Hour contract lost because Basie was Black
86.s: John Hammond arranged for Basie to do the Camel Hour, but the sponsor's head refused a Black band.
86.ch: Road tales, then Cleveland, St. Louis and Harlem
86.q: think very few people know this except the older guys, Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and myself, we’re the only ones left of the Basie band. They remember, but John Hammond, he was responsible for the Count Basie band, period, because he brought Basie to New York. They had, you remember, the Camel Hour,…

86.t: Breaking the color line in the ABC Hollywood Palace band
86.s: He was the first Black musician in the Mitchell Ayres band, hired partly to integrate it.
86.q: Well, the Hollywood Palace, ABC, and I think that they were looking for somebody. It didn’t have to be me, just thank God it was me. And I was blessed. Mitchell Ayres was the bandleader. I was the first black musician to be in the band on ABC and the time was just right. I think they were looking…

86.s: He says he met no hostility from white studio players.
86.q: Never. If they did, they didn’t let me know anything about it. Because I had a lot of fun with all the guys that I recorded with, every one. We had big laughs. When I see some of them now, they all reiterate something funny, some incident that happened, something that I was a part of. So it was…

367.t: Tonight Show trumpeters and Bernie Glow
367.s: Young recalls Clark Terry, Jimmy Maxwell, Johnny Frosk and first trumpeter Bernie Glow, who wrote an article about him.
367.q: Tonight Show Band? Let‘s see, Clark Terry… Jimmy Maxwell … I can‘t think of these other two guys, I‘m seeing them, but I can‘t call their names… I can‘t call their names, I‘ll just hold you up trying to think …

367.t: Tonight Show schedule left evenings free for other bands
367.s: Young explains the show's rehearsal and one-hour taping left time to play with Thad and Mel in New York and with other bands in Los Angeles.
367.q: You start, I think the rehearsal was three o‘clock. Three, four, five, six, you rehearsed. The rehearsal would be three to four. Then they have… how was that? You would have about an hour off then you come and do the Show, and the Show would go for one hour, no longer, it would go one hour. You‘d…

367.s: Young recalls Johnny Carson joking with him and sitting in on drums at rehearsals.
367.q: [laughs] Yeah, but, Johnny now Johnny, he used to kid me a lot, he made a few jokes about something I wish I could think of what it was, it was about Snooky. I can‘t but, Johnny he treated me nice. He treated all the guys nice. Every now and then he

367.t: Tommy Newsom, the square-looking saxophonist and arranger
367.s: Young recalls Tommy Newsom, whom Johnny Carson teased, as a sweet man and close friend.
367.q: Yes you do. He was the leader. Sometimes when Doc wasn‘t there he would be the leader and he would be so square looking …

367.t: Whether he was Doc Severinsen's high-note safety net
367.s: Young denies ever covering high notes for Doc Severinsen and says Doc had chops.
367.q: I never had to hit no high notes for Doc. Doc had…

367.t: The Jones brothers and juggling the NBC and Thad-Mel jobs
367.s: Young jokes about Elvin and Hank Jones and says there was no conflict between the Tonight Show and the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band, which worked from another studio.
367.q: And Hank, you know, Hank was playing in that band when it first started, but I don‘t know, he didn‘t stay it long. I don‘t know why he didn‘t stay or anything, I have no idea, but he was in that first band. He was in that band, man, Hank.

65.t: Live broadcasts from La Conga and the theme "Nague"
65.s: The band began broadcasting in 1942, opening with "Nague" in a John Bartee arrangement.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: Because it was, it had a good message.

65.s: They recorded forty or fifty shows for the army at La Conga, a studio and the Palladium, with four-hour sessions; he also mentions Muzak.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Well, it was in -- "Saludos Amigos" was recorded in La Conga and it was recorded in a studio for the army, and then we did few recordings at Palladium Ballroom, in 1947 and we did a few recordings from La Conga, where the Casablanca is now, that was Birdland, we made a recording for the army.

65.s: He knew Chano Pozo from the CMQ and Cadena Azul stations.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: ....and then in Cadena Azul, it was where actually he was working with the owner of that - he was the baby of that particular station....

65.t: Fred Robbins and Latin music on radio
65.s: Disc jockey Fred Robbins played the instrumental "Killer Joe" because he could not play Spanish vocals to his jazz audience.
65.ch: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
65.q: .....instrumental, so he had a chance. He was a very good friend on my band list, there was no question. He was a good friend of mine or he is a good friend of mine, and he like latin music, but you know, he was Jazz-oriented. He just can't play over the radio somebody singing in Spanish. He lose…

65.t: Jack Robbins and the coast-to-coast midnight broadcasts
65.s: Publisher Jack Robbins arranged radio time from La Conga to plug the music he published; few air checks survive.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: Well, Jack Robbins in account that he had the publishing house, all the publishing house was helping the radio station.....

65.t: Last days in Los Angeles; Pagani's publicity and "El Bongo Arrollador"
65.s: Federico Pagani handled publicity and set up twenty or so live broadcasts; they recorded the Bongo number with Verne.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Three months with us and then when we came back here he stayed there about another three months because, you know, he is smart in publicity and propaganda or whatever you want to call it and he stayed there. He helped us a lot because he helped to make the publicity; so all the posters and - you…

901.t: Second to Doc Severinsen in network TV gigs
901.s: Rowe notes Chez ranks near Doc Severinsen for network TV tenure; Chez mentions other TV band players such as Mark Pender.
901.q: TV. Network TV. And there’s been a lot of guys, man. There was a guy from Lawrence Welk, he was on forever. The guys from the Conan band, Conan just got rid of his band, but they were on cable. So that’s Mark Pender. I play in a band with Mark here in New Jersey.

901.s: Chez recalls improvising songs on the spot when the band was asked for a song name.
901.q: Yeah. That was top of my head. Just kind of yeah, improv it, just kind of improv. And they would come up with a name of a song and you’d be like yeah, I know that song, and you would make up your own song. You know country. [Scats] you know and you’d just come up with some weird lyrics to it. So…

901.t: Talkback mic, band conversations and Martin Short songs
901.s: Chez did not want to lead; the band used a switch on the vocal mic to pick songs during breaks, the producers borrowed their hair piece banter, and Paul wrote songs for Martin Short.
901.q: No. That’s a lot. That was a toughie because there’s so many different things going on. You know what, we — I didn’t want to but we all kind of did, because what we did on those instance where I didn’t know what Simple Gifts means, we had ear monitors and then we had a microphone. And I had a…

901.t: Sweeps hire and getting the Letterman job on air
901.s: After touring with Tower of Power and the Robert Cray Band, Chez was hired for sweeps and Letterman said on air that the kid stays; the 17 years gave him a pension.
901.ch: Getting and negotiating the Letterman job
901.q: So then when they moved to CBS I was out on the West Coast playing with Tower of Power and the Robert Cray Band. And I did that for a while. I came back home and I called Shaffer up and I said, “I really don’t want to go on the road anymore,” You know Tom Malone was playing trumpet and trombone.…

901.t: Letterman playing drums and Chez singing Free Bird
901.s: Letterman lived in Montana, loved the band, played drums daily at rehearsal, and made Chez sing Free Bird on his last show.
901.q: Yeah. He’s out in Montana, that’s where he is. Him and Tom Brokaw bought two farms in the middle of Montana back to back. So if you look at a map I think the whole middle of the state of Montana is owned by Letterman/Brokaw.

215.t: Tonight Show schedule and playing without rehearsal
215.s: He split the week with Tony Mottola; Skitch never rehearsed and players arrived from other sessions just in time for the theme.
215.q: We did five days a week, but I used to split that up with Tony Mottola who was on staff. He’d do two nights, I’d do three nights. And if we had a recording I would sub for him, I would go in and do his night and then he’d make it up another time.

215.t: V-discs, transcriptions and radio shows with Vaughn Monroe
215.s: Making V-discs and 15-minute direct-to-disc transcriptions, then the Fitch and Camel radio shows with Slam Stewart, Benny Goodman Trio and the Basie rhythm section.
215.q: Yeah. And we even made those big ones, they were like 15 minute transcriptions. And it’s like direct to disc. That’s what it was. And we had to play 15 minutes without making a mistake.

215.t: Kate Smith Show staff job at NBC after Vaughan Monroe
215.s: After the Monroe band broke up, Bucky got an NBC staff job on the Kate Smith Show through a cellist; he talks pay and security, and never wanting to do anything else.
215.q: I was finished with the big band. Vaughan broke up then. I went back to New York and luckily I got a job as a staff musician playing for the “Kate Smith Show.”

215.t: Kate Smith Show on NBC television
215.s: He joined the Kate Smith show on Maurice Brown's tip, earning $250 a week with a short daily rehearsal.
215.ch: New York studio and TV work
215.q: Yeah, well I was on about three different times on NBC. I mean when I left Vaughn Monroe I went right on NBC with the Kate Smith Show. And that was live, five days a

215.t: Goofy gigs: Tiny Tim's wedding and Ryan's Hope
215.s: He tuned Tiny Tim's ukulele on The Tonight Show wedding and played guitar for a soap-opera actress with a stand-in on camera.
215.q: Oh I know. Another thing on the soap opera “Ryan’s Hope” once I did, I got called to play for Helen Gallagher or somebody, one of those great actresses that used to do the show. And the producer had me come in with my guitar and he says, “Well can you find another guitar that looks like yours?” I…

356.t: Moving into live TV and sitcoms
356.s: Steve Allen gave his first break; then The Nuthouse and a series of sitcoms, including The Girl With Something Extra.
356.q: Well I auditioned for a show — well first of all I went in with Steve Allen. He gave me my first break and I’d done some material off the comedy album that I’d done for Capitol Records. And then from that I got a show called “The Nuthouse,” and I did a routine called “Hunting with a Falcon.” And…

356.t: The Merv Griffin Show with Pete Candoli
356.s: Funny moments on Merv's show and working with Candoli on the theme and in Las Vegas.
356.q: Well there would be just funny stuff, yeah. I remember, and Pete Candoli, we worked together on Merv’s show for like twenty years. And Pete, we’d play in Las Vegas, we played an hour and a half show and it was all acts. And I don’t know, I’d be exhausted playing third trumpet, and Pete would always…

356.s: An easy schedule, freedom to take off, substitutes, and comfort in front of cameras.
356.q: Yeah, great, really great. It was an easy job. We went in at 4:30 and we were through at 8:30. We’d work three days a week I think.

356.s: Favorite comedians and celebrities he met, including Lucille Ball, Oscar Peterson and Bernadette Peters.
356.q: Well I always liked George Carlin and just the real good comics I loved to see, Richard Pryor and Woody Allen and those guys. Well that’s the thing about Merv’s show that was so great, you got to meet everybody, all the great people. I got to meet Lucille Ball. She was great. She would always say,…

356.t: Comedy with Julie London and Jack Marshall
356.s: Comedy grew out of working with Julie London and Bobby Troup, and he wrote comedy with Jack Marshall and made a Capitol album.
356.ch: Comedy, Lenny Bruce and early jobs
356.q: Yes. I was working with Julie London and Bobby Troup. Bobby Troup just passed away you know, last Sunday night. We’re going to do a memorial with my big band, and Supersax and Page Cavanaugh. But I was working with Bobby Troup and Julie London. We were working at Mr. Kelly’s in Chicago. And she…

589.t: Yvonne Daniels and how he got into radio
589.s: After a conversational interview on Yvonne Daniels' show, a station manager asks Lewis to consider radio.
589.q: Good. Yvonne Daniels lived in Chicago. I think she was from St. Louis, but she lived in Chicago. She had been in radio down there. She moved up here, and she became a force in radio. This is after Daddy-O Daylie. She had a morning show. As I recall, she was on a station that played George Duke, Wes…

589.t: The weekend show Jazz: Ramsey and Yvonne, and its syndication
589.s: The two-hour show grew to many stations, Daniels died, and it was later syndicated as Legends of Jazz.
589.q: the engineer sitting over there. But you’re talking to hundreds of thousands of people, as the case is in Chicago. I just couldn’t – I couldn’t fathom that. So I said, “I don’t know.” He says, “Think about it. Let me know.” I thought about, and I didn’t let him know. But he called me, and he said,…

589.t: Hosting a jazz show on BET with Bob Johnson
589.s: Lewis called Bob Johnson after BET kept replaying a Montreal concert and was asked to host a low-budget jazz show.
589.q: Yeah. This goes way back. Where do you find this? This goes way back. Every now and then I’m going through the t.v. – you know how you scroll and you look. I would always check out BET, see what’s going on, because I had met Bob Johnson casually somewhere. Once I had met him, I started checking out…

589.t: Legends of Jazz grows from radio to PBS television
589.s: A Cadillac tour fell through but WTTW agreed to a 13-episode Legends of Jazz TV series.
589.q: Yeah. The Legends of Jazz radio show I think grew up to 80 or 90 stations across the country, whatever it was. The question was, what do we do now? I had a bright idea of a Legends of Jazz tour. One of our sponsors was Cadillac. Before I called Cadillac, I talked to Larry Rosen. Larry Rosen had…

589.t: Guesting on Billy Taylor's CBS Sunday Morning segment
589.s: Lewis recalls being honored to appear with Taylor on Sunday Morning in 1997.
589.q: Yeah. I’m trying to separate now from others, but I can’t bring the actual performance to mind, because I keep mixing it with those other – with the ones on Bravo, and then the ones we did after that. That particular event – I know I was very, very impressed and honored that he called, asked me to…

227.s: Mandel became a staff arranger at the WMGM radio station, brought in Billy Byers, and began writing strings and dramatic music for radio plays.
227.ch: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
227.q: In about 1949, then I got a job, I started getting into what was commercial music, I mean in the sense that I was curious about writing for strings and things and I got an opportunity to go with the last of the radio station bands. WMGM used to be here used to be at 711 Fifth Avenue and I became a…

227.t: Writing for Your Show of Shows
227.s: Mandel and Irwin Kostal supplied live weekly music for Sid Caesar's 90-minute show, an education in strings, dancers and visual cues.
227.ch: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
227.q: Your Show of Shows, Irwin Kostal called me and the two of us turned out the music there for a long time for that show. Irv did most of the work, Irwin not Irving, but everybody always called him Irv, he was just a miracle worker, doing that show was a whole other thing, it was very exciting.

227.t: Ben Casey, Mister Roberts and the Andy Williams show
227.s: Mandel recalls TV episodes and the live Andy Williams variety show where he met Dave Grusin and joked with Williams's perfect ears.
227.ch: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
227.q: Yeah, I did that. I didn't do much, I think I subbed for Frank Perkins a few times while he was ill, he was having an operation of some kind, but that was his show. He's the guy who wrote, “Stars Fell on Alabama.”

227.t: How Mandel, Cohn and Kahn worked together
227.s: The three arrangers played each other their charts at the piano; Mandel dates the Elliot Lawrence writing from 1952, after radio and television work.
227.ch: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
227.q: Oh, beautifully, you know ‘cause we’d all known each other for a long time before that and were in other bands and all that sort of stuff. And we used to always play each other our arrangements on the piano and all that, you know, we hung.

227.t: Sid Caesar the saxophonist and the timeline
227.s: Mandel notes that Caesar was a modest saxophonist who jammed with them, and dates the Show of Shows period to 1950-52.
227.ch: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
227.q: Nothing, nothing in terms of that, but he was a hell of a good guy and a great comedian. And he used to come and jam with us, I jammed with him a couple times up in the mountains and he played kind of a watered-down Charlie Barnet style of saxophone. And he was always on himself, you know he just…

64.t: Impromptu with Jim Hall; becoming musical director of NET's jazz series
64.s: He made the album Impromptu, then in 1958 became musical director of the first educational television series on jazz at NBC using staff musicians.
64.ch: Television, education and radio in the 1960s

64.t: The Subject Is Jazz television series
64.s: He discusses the series' host, guests and quality, and distinguishes it from CBS's The Sound of Jazz.
64.ch: Television, education and radio in the 1960s

And he felt… he really honestly was never convinced that jazz was America’s classical music and that it was indeed something that was not only…

64.t: Moving to WNEW, salary and balancing radio with playing

64.ch: Television, education and radio in the 1960s

413.t: Hinton at CBS in jeans and Percy Faith's dark suit

413.ch: Young players, schools and studio work

I've got two dark suits and two black ties and that's going to have to last me until I die. You know, there was a time when I think -- even…

413.t: Staff pay and who held staff jobs

413.q: Right. Well, first off, the staff musicians got a lower pay than the outside musicians, but the consideration was it was a weekly salary and it was supposed to be a lifetime job, you know. Nobody foresaw that eventually they would cut down. And they had to employ 65 musicians for the networks and…

413.q: Well, I went into -- see, I left Benny Goodman in 1943 and I went into CBS, what they called the staff orchestra which was -- you know, in those days it was just radio and they had what they called staff orchestras. That

238.t: Being the subject of This Is Your Life

238.ch: This Is Your Life and film work

238.s: She telegraphed disc jockey Frank Bull, who read it on air and invited her onto his hour.

238.ch: This Is Your Life and film work

238.ch: This Is Your Life and film work

239.t: Scoring the pilot of That Was the Week That Was

239.t: The Subject Is Jazz with Gilbert Seldes and Billy Taylor

Oh, Jimmy Cleveland. And my job was to give an example -- we had different guests every week, and my job was to…

239.s: Short notes on the Lena Horne, Carol Burnett, Jack Paar and Mr. Broadway shows, and a vocal group that did not know the Negro national anthem.

239.q: Yeah. And it came off well, because we used it on the, 'Love You Madly,' TV show. That was another good team to work with, with Quincy Jones, Phil Moore, Luther Henderson, Marvin Hamlisch. I don't mean to just drop names, but --

239.t: Helping Tonight Show bands with the acts he writes for

239.q: And with Joe Williams, Shirley Horn -- who else? A couple of other acts that I had been doing albums with, and I would go over to the studio with them.

598.t: Moving into studio and television work

598.q: Yeah. 598.t: Doc Severinsen, Carson and the band

He would always come and listen to us rehearse, and he knew every one of us, and always went out of his way to be good to us. You know very few people…

598.t: Show guests: Cloris Leachman and Rodney Dangerfield
598.s: Candoli recalls Leachman's singing, Rickles, and Dangerfield doing private comedy for the band.

Rickles was hilarious you know. And I’m trying to think of some of the other comics and off hand I can’t recall.…

598.s: He recalls Mickey Rooney drunk, Carson and Streisand, and an actor who died the day after taping.

209.t: Where the band sat on live TV variety shows

Carol Burnett, there was the audience, here is the audience here and here’s the stage here, and the band was right here, abutting onto the stage but on the side of the audience behind a glass. You could see the audience but it had glass up there to keep the…

209.t: Seven years on the Dean Martin Show and the theme tenor solo
209.s: He recalls the collapsible piano gag and was on the show seven years. He played the prominent tenor solo on the theme, which Les Brown's road tenor was often credited for.
209.q: I think the show was on ten years, and I was on there seven. And when the staff orchestra ended then I left because I got a chance to do the Carol Burnett Show, which was a better paying show. And as a matter of fact I had a tenor solo on the theme of the Dean Martin show that was very prominent,…

209.t: Hearing himself on reruns and the Laugh-In cast
209.s: Laugh-In was re-shown for months, paying high re-use percentages, and he sometimes recognises his playing. He praises the cast, including Goldie Hawn, Arte Johnson and JoAnne Worley.
209.q: Occasionally, yeah occasionally, in some old pictures. And they did re-show, the Laugh- In series was on six years, and that was re-shown over a period of eight months, five nights a week. And that was very lucrative. Because those were the first re-showings, so as I told you the percentages were…

209.t: How live variety shows were produced, and their decline
209.s: Shows were done in two days with pre-recorded music and two taped performances, so the band sat watching. The shows shared one format, over-exposed guests, and no musical variety shows exist now.
209.q: Well I’ll tell you the way — almost all live television shows were done the same. They were done in two days. 153.q: A regular big band: four trumpets – sometimes five trumpets – four ’bones, five reeds, piano, bass, and drums. Once in a while we had a guitar player. No percussion player.

406.t: Four years on the ABC staff: conductors and the reed section

406.t: WOR's Endorsed by Dorsey show and organizing Sy Oliver's band
406.s: After WOR with Sy Oliver he helped Oliver, fresh from Dorsey's band, organize his new band for the Zanzibar, bringing in players like George Dorsey.
406.q: after I did the Dorsey Show with Cy we -- Cy and I got together to organize that band he had. He didn't know any musicians because he had just come out of Tommy Dorsey's band so he --

677.t: Recording with Gleason, off-Broadway shows and joining CBS
677.s: After Ellington he recorded with Jackie Gleason, played Nancy Walker and Carol Channing shows, and joined the CBS staff after Hodges retired.
677.ch: Europe 1933, New York Cotton Club, Hodges group

Not only recorded with Ellington -- I recorded with so many other groups and things that I get all -- you know I…

677.q: Oh, yes. I had been over to the studios and finally got a call. CBS come -- there was a vacancy, I remember, on staff, and I got the job.

677.ch: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
677.q: Well, there were many of them which would be recognized in certain places, but they seem to keep every man sort of equal. There weren't any terrific stars as you would call them.

677.t: Father comes around and radio broadcasts
677.s: His father gradually listened to Brown's melodic playing on the radio; the Cotton Club broadcast nightly without pay.
677.q: when we were broadcasting, and he would turn his back to the radio. So finally he got so he'd turn around and listen, because I didn't -- I leaned more to the melodic type of playing instead of the raucous jazz type. Although I could. And he would finally listen. Then as I would come back to L. A.…

17.t: Leaving Cab for Raymond Scott's CBS staff
17.ch: Big bands, small groups and studio work
17.q: Well that was a great experience. See I was one of the first black drummers to be on staff at CBS. There was four of us altogether.

17.q: Yeah, see, and I just went on and did my thing and he done his thing, you know, because we did several things on the Tonight Show before Johnny Carson got it—Steve Allen—we were on there and did a thing together. 17.t: Black musicians on the CBS staff

17.q: Well yes, and then they were trying to get that thing going there, John Hammond, so you didn't think too much about it, you know, because it wasn't any sort of prejudice or anything else evident up there when you were playing, because they all treated you beautiful. 17.t: How John Hammond got him the CBS job and Carmen Jones
17.ch: Big bands, small groups and studio work
17.q: Lou Shuby, he was the contractor for all of the bands at CBS. Of course John Hammond was the instigator. He's the one that told me about it.

380.t: Becoming a disk jockey on KHON and the sextet's tenor player
380.s: He was trained by Larry Grant as a DJ on a Honolulu AM station and sneaked jazz in, and names Pete Peterson on tenor.

380.q: Oh, after that, let's see... I have to get a list of all the shows that I was involved in then. What's her name, Jo Diamond? 428.q: Barbara, Alfred and Nancy. And I started working in -- I was doing work on a higher plane than, -- I was working at the Blue Angel, and -- and I started in the theater, was doing a TV show with Hazel Scott on a regular basis and --

96.q: Well actually, to me it was verbose it was fun, you know. I'm a character at times anyway. I like to talk and it was fun. And I worked quite hard on the thing. I got in good shape physically and excercised, plenty of exercises and studied my lines at home. And I knew the part quite well. And to me…

168.t: Playing in groups of several basses; the Pat Boone Show
168.s: His only multi-bass work was a late-1950s Pat Boone Show appearance with several bassists.
168.q: No, I've never really worked on that scale, but I do remember I've been on a couple of shows where there were several bass players. This particular show I'm thinking about is the Pat Boone Show and that was in the late '50s, where there were several basses doing our thing on this show with…

611.t: Broadcasting semi-classical music with Bowles, Curl and Eddie Barrow
611.s: The four-piece Bowles group broadcast three times a week for Howard's Clothing Company, playing semi-classical pieces such as 'Nola', probably the first Black band to do commercial radio in Boston.
611.q: Well, that Harry Carney deal, see, came in from me broadcastin' three days a week with Curl, see. And we were doing mostly technical solo work, I mean, it wasn't so much jazz much, it was semi-classical stuff. I give you an idea - I was playin' things like "Nola" on the saxophone, alto, and Curl…

427.t: The Sunset Club on Twelfth Street, Piney Brown and the radio breakfast show
427.s: At Piney Brown's Sunset Club, Turner did a five a.m. radio breakfast show heard as far as New York.
427.ch: Black and Tan and Kansas City nightlife
427.q: I met Pete when I was a young man but we went... John Hammond, after we moved to Twelfth Street... We move out on Twelfth Street, a joint called the Sunset Club, and they had a fellow runnin' it called Piney Brown.

74.t: Hammond's CBS Jam Session and the Nineteenth Hole
74.s: Mosley takes part in a linked CBS blues broadcast and Hammond brings Krupa's trombonists to the Nineteenth Hole.
74.ch: Leading his own band in New York
74.q: Oscar Levant. Oscar Levant was playing piano-- anyway it was on Jam Session, we did the blues. That was after Johnny had come out to Barnes Tavern and he got really in my corner and one night after we got down to a place called the Nineteenth Hole--

149.t: The '20th Century Gabriel' name and the broadcasts
149.s: An NBC announcer coined the name and Hawkins did coast-to-coast broadcasts, including from the Lincoln Hotel.
149.q: I was in the Savoy Ballroom doing an NBC broadcast. And, this was in the afternoon. And, the announcer at that time, he brought us on. I had this tune, "Swing Out", composed by Avery Parrish, you know. I had a kind of cadenza like that I played before the tune started swinging. So, when I started…

6.t: Kirby's classical repertoire, Sunday broadcasts and heavy schedule
6.s: He agrees the classics were chosen partly for ASCAP public domain reasons; the band did a Sunday sustaining radio program with little rehearsal, a record date and a transcription session every month.
6.q: Yes. That's true. Yes. Then we had a sustaining program. We broadcast every Sunday around -- I think it was 12:00 or 1:00 o'clock on Sunday afternoon. And of course it required a lot of music, you know. Every Sunday was a different program. And the band wasn't -- wasn't very old then. I would say…

115.t: Street singing and the 'Store Without a Name' radio show
115.s: The quartet sang for tips on the streets and broadcast every morning imitating the Mills Brothers for about $25.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: at these little places, they'd have little stands. And guys would come and throw us money and give us money and like that.

75.t: Amalgamated radio broadcasts and the Palmer Brothers group
75.s: He recalls the band's "Trouble in Paradise" radio number and an earlier group with the Palmer Brothers and John Kirby broadcasting on the Amalgamated network.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: : Yeah, possibly. Our big number was 'Trouble In Paradise' over the Amalgamated Radio! As a matter of fact, that's the second time... I don't know if it was before... Was it before...? I was playing with the Palmer Brothers. When John Kirby left Fletcher's band, he organized a group with the Palmer…

124.s: Chick's band made radio transcriptions that stopped without explanation as hotels piped in softer music.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Yeah. We did that in New York. I just ran across some articles on some of the things that we had done, you know. We used to do a lot of stuff like that. And all of sudden, they cut that out. We didn't do too much of that.

76.t: Connie's Inn under Allie Ross and the WOR commercial program
76.s: Zutty went into Connie's Inn with Allie Ross's band and had one of the first commercial radio programs by a Black band, on WOR for a clothing store. Marge and Zutty argue whether it was Dickerson's men.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: And then the next job, when you really started working was in Connie's Inn. That's when we sent for mother and I to come.

78.t: Rehearsing for WBBM broadcasts and clearing programs
78.s: Half-hour broadcasts of about eight tunes had to be submitted to WBBM librarian Helen Keppler a week ahead for clearance; rehearsals scheduled around the men, who had no day jobs.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: Oh yes. We would have to rehearse because I used to have to turn my programs in to WBBM, you know, a week in advance to have them cleared, you know, like what were the original things and the tunes that couldn't be broadcast at that time, and I would make arrangements, you know, musical…

171.t: Chicken in the basket song and Vine Street Varieties
171.s: Ramey's jingle on 'Pennies from Heaven', the Saturday show at the Lincoln Theater and Dave Dexter's fondness for McShann.
171.ch: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
171.q: He took care of business very good at the Martins, and in fact they loved him out there. We made a tune -- they had a special food that they were promoting, chicken in the basket. And I made up a song on it, on "Pennies from Heaven," you know. I put some other words to it.

13.s: Announcer Ted Pearson began calling him Father Hines on air.
13.ch: Joining Earl Hines and the Grand Terrace
13.q: Earl "Fatha" Hines. I don't know where he got that father from. Then after he'd make the announcement, then George Dixon's the one started hollering, "Father Hines, Father Hines."

79.t: Small-group dates and the Blues in the Night broadcast
79.s: His own group played the Waldorf and a six-piece WOR broadcast tied to the Warner Brothers film Blues in the Night.
79.ch: The 1940s: small groups, Teddy Wilson and Ethel Waters
